_readme: What a sealed Pokemon product is SUPPOSED to cost, so somebody standing in a
shop can work out how far over retail they are being asked to pay.
READ THIS FIRST, BECAUSE IT CHANGES WHAT YOU CAN PUT IN HERE.
WHAT AN MSRP IS, AND THIS FILE GOT IT WRONG UNTIL 17 AUGUST 2026. MSRP is the
manufacturer's SUGGESTED retail price. Pokemon Center is The Pokemon
Company's own shop selling its own product, so the price it sells at IS the
price the manufacturer suggests. That is the whole of what an MSRP is. There
is no separate document to go looking for.
This file used to say 'The Pokemon Company does not publish an MSRP list' and
the page repeated it in three places. What two research passes actually found
was that no DOCUMENT TITLED MSRP exists: pokemon.com's product showcases
itemise contents and state no price, and press.pokemon.com carries none
either. That is a true finding and it was written up as something much
bigger, which made the page hedge about whether the number existed at all.
It does. It is on Pokemon's own shop.
SO A POKEMON CENTER READING IS THE STRONGEST EVIDENCE THIS PAGE HAS, not one
source among several. Where it disagrees with a hobbyist reference table,
Pokemon Center wins outright and the page says so without hedging.
AND A SUGGESTION IS ALL IT IS, which is the point of the page rather than a
caveat on it. No law makes a shop honor it. Retailers set their own prices
and are free to charge what they like, which is why the same box is $49.99
from Pokemon and several times that somewhere else.
THE 17 AUGUST 2026 READINGS. The site answers a script with a ~1KB bot-check
page and no product data, so it was read BY A PERSON IN A REAL BROWSER off
its own TCG cards category page. That happened TWICE on the day: a first pass
of 31 products which wrongly believed it had the whole category, and a second
that walked all ten pages and collected 400 more. The two sets do not overlap
by a single product path. All 431 readings live in
data/pokemon-center-prices.json with the product path and the date on each
one, and rows here join to that file by exact name through `pcFrom` rather
than re-typing a figure. DO NOT FETCH THE SITE, do not automate a re-read,
and do not use its images.
EVERY PRICE HERE IS STILL A DATED READING AND THE PAGE SAYS SO ON EVERY ROW.
A shop price can change, including Pokemon's own: booster bundles went from
$23.94 to $26.94, and the Pokemon Center ETB from $54.99 to $59.99. Confident
about what the figure IS, precise about WHEN it was read.
A ROW ONLY GETS A `price` WHEN ONE OF THESE IS TRUE:
a) it is a Pokemon Center price, which is the manufacturer's own shop and
therefore the manufacturer's suggestion, or
b) at least TWO independent sources print the SAME figure to the cent.
(a) IS THE STRONG ONE AND (b) IS THE FALLBACK. A row on (b) is careful people
reading shop listings and agreeing, which is good evidence rather than the
manufacturer speaking. The page labels the two differently for that reason.
Anything else leaves `price` null. A null price is NOT printed, ever. The
page shows the row with the reason instead, and where the sources disagree
it shows the spread they disagree across, clearly marked as a spread rather
than a number to hold a shop to.
A POKEMON CENTER READING OUTRANKS A REFERENCE, AND THE PAGE SAYS SO OUT LOUD
WHEN THEY DIFFER. It wins under rule (a), and it does not get to bury the
source it beat: put the loser in `disagreesWith` and the row prints both,
named and dated. The reader gets told which one is the manufacturer and which
one is a compilation. Quietly dropping the loser is the failure this whole
file is built to avoid.
POKEMON CENTER SELLS TEN YEARS OF BACK CATALOGUE BESIDE THIS MONTH'S BOX, so
ONE PRODUCT TYPE AT TWO PRICES ON ONE DAY IS THE NORMAL CASE HERE, not the
exception. Thirty one readings hid that. Four hundred and thirty one make it
the first thing you meet. Build & Battle Boxes are listed at $19.99 and at
$21.99. Sleeved packs at $3.99 and $4.49. Display boxes at $143.64 and at
$161.64. Mini tins at $8.99 and $9.99.
THE TEST IS WHETHER THE SPLIT IS GENERATIONAL, AND THE ERA PREFIX IN THE
READING FILE IS WHAT ANSWERS IT. Every $19.99 Build & Battle Box is a
'Sword & Shield-' one and every $21.99 is a 'Scarlet & Violet-' or
'Mega Evolution-' one, with no overlap at all. That is a price rise with old
stock still on the shelf, so the row prints the CURRENT figure and NAMES the
older one in its note. A reader holding this month's box gets the number they
need, and a reader holding a 2022 box is told why theirs is cheaper.
WHERE TWO PRICES ARE LIVE INSIDE THE CURRENT LINE, COUNT THE LISTINGS AND
WEIGH THEM. THIS RULE USED TO SAY THE ROW PRINTS NOTHING, FULL STOP, AND
THAT WAS TOO BLUNT: it left the display box row blank while twelve current
boxes in Pokemon's own shop agreed to the cent. A blanket rule is not
judgement, and the reader pays for the difference.
A LOPSIDED SPLIT IS AN ANSWER. Twelve current display boxes at $161.64 and
ONE, Temporal Forces, fifty cents under them, is not two prices. It is one
price and an outlier. Print the figure the listings agree on and NAME the
odd one in the row's note, where somebody holding that exact box will read
it. Burying it would be dishonest. Refusing to answer because of it is a
different failure and it is the one this file actually made.
A GENUINE SPLIT IS NOT AN ANSWER. Five Tech Sticker Collections at $14.99
and five at $15.99. Four stacking tins at $12.99 and three at $14.99.
Premium Collections at $39.99, $49.99 and $59.99. Ultra Premium
Collections at $119.99 against $179.99. Nothing in any of those is an
outlier and there is no figure to print. DO NOT AVERAGE THEM AND DO NOT
PICK THE ONE THAT APPEARS MORE OFTEN.
AND SAY WHICH KIND OF BLANK IT IS, because the two look identical on the
page and are not the same claim. A row whose price VARIES BY PRODUCT
carries `varies: true` and says so in plain words in `blank`: somebody did
the research and the finding is that the type has no one price. That is an
answer, not a gap, and the page prints 'Varies by product' over it rather
than a phrase that reads as nobody having looked. Leave `varies` off the
rows that really are thin, like the single-pack blister resting on one
seven year old listing, and let those say 'Not sourced'.
AND VERIFY THE PRODUCT TYPE BEFORE PAIRING ON A NAME. Pokemon Center never
writes the word blister, so the three-pack row rests on a listing called
'3 Booster Packs & Promo Card', which IS a three-pack blister. A loose pack
and a sleeved pack are different SKUs sold side by side. 'V Battle Deck' at
$29.99 is the two-deck versus box and not the $14.99 single deck. Two
different SKUs are both called 'V Heroes Tin (Espeon V)' at two prices. A
similar name is not a match, and a display box cannot be priced by
multiplying a pack.
ONE READING IS ONE PRODUCT, AND THAT LIMIT IS REAL. Two Tech Sticker
Collections at $14.99 is evidence about Tech Sticker Collections. The two
Ultra-Premium Collections at $119.99 are a fact about those two boxes and
not about the type, because the same type runs to $179.99 elsewhere, so that
row still carries no price. If a type genuinely varies, a store reading is a
data point in its spread and not an answer. That is the OPPOSITE end of the
same judgement the display box row makes: twelve agreeing beats one outlier,
two agreeing does not settle a type a third source prices sixty dollars
higher.
THIS IS A PAGE ABOUT PRICES BEING WRONG. A wrong number on it is worse than
a missing one. If you are not sure, leave it null.
Per row, and only these five are yours to fill in:
price       the number, in US dollars, no currency symbol. null if not
sourced. The page omits the price on any row that is null.
source      who said so, in words, e.g. 'Pokemon Center' or the site name
sourceUrl   the exact page you read it on. Leave it '' on a row that has
`pcFrom`: the builder fills it in from the product path.
readOn      the date YOU read it, ISO, e.g. '2026-08-17'. Not the date the
page claims to have been updated.
priceKind   'store' if it is Pokemon's own shop price, which is the
manufacturer's suggestion and the strong case. 'refs' if it is
a figure two or more price references agree on, which is the
fallback. Decides the label the page prints over the number.
Supporting fields, optional:
pcFrom      [name, ...] exact `name` strings in
data/pokemon-center-prices.json. THE BUILDER CHECKS THEM: a
name that is not in that file, a name that two SKUs share at
different prices, or a reading whose price is not this row's
price, FAILS THE BUILD. It also fills in sourceUrl from the
first product's path, and the page says how many listings
carried the figure. Use it for every store price, so a number
on the page is never re-typed from a reading. LIST EVERY
LISTING THAT AGREES rather than a token two: the count is the
evidence, and it is what tells a later editor whether a figure
rested on one box or on thirty seven.
agrees      [{source, url, readOn}] everything else that printed the same
figure. The page counts these, so a row backed by four sources
says so and a row backed by two says that instead.
disagreesWith  [{amount, source, url, readOn, as}] on a row that HAS a
price: who prints a different figure. The page names them and
their number under the row, so a store price does not silently
overwrite a reference. Never use it to hide a real conflict.
disagree    [{amount, source, url, readOn, as}] used when price is null and
the sources conflict. The page prints the spread and names
them all. Do not use this to sneak a number past the rule.
blank       a short phrase saying why price is null, in plain words. It is
printed. e.g. 'sources disagree', 'only one source found'.
varies      true when the reason there is no price is that the TYPE does
not have one: several current products, several prices, no
outlier. The page then prints 'Varies by product' over the row
instead of 'Not sourced', because those are different findings
and only one of them is a hole in the research. See the rule
above. Do not set it on a row that is simply thin.
note        one sentence of context, printed under the row.
Fields the builder owns and you should leave alone:
id          matches shared/taxonomy.mjs PRODUCT_TYPES where a tag exists,
so the row can link to /openings/<id>.html
packsFrom   the exact `productName` in data/pack-counts-current.json. The
pack count and the 'seen listed at' figure are both read from
there, so this site states a pack count in ONE place. A name
that does not match prints nothing rather than a guess.
ADDING A ROW: copy an existing one, set price to null, and give it a `what`.
scripts/build-msrp.mjs holds the photo pin for each id in its PHOTOS map; a
row with no pin renders with the site's no-photo hatch rather than a hole.
A ROW IS ONLY WORTH ADDING IF A SHOPPER WOULD PLAUSIBLY MEET THAT PRODUCT ON
A SHELF. Pokemon Center also sells pencil cases, erasers bundled with two
packs, mini portfolios and poster tubes, all of them priced and none of them
the thing somebody is being overcharged for.
NEVER STATE OR IMPLY PULL RATES HERE OR ON THE PAGE. Site-wide rule.

pokemon-center.name: Pokemon Center
pokemon-center.what: The Pokemon Company's own shop, selling its own product. Its price is the manufacturer's suggested retail price, which is what MSRP means, so this is the strongest source on the page and the only one that is the manufacturer rather than somebody reading listings. Its TCG cards category was read in a real browser on 17 August 2026, in two passes: 31 products first, then all ten pages of it for 400 more, none of which repeated a product from the first pass. All 431 are recorded in data/pokemon-center-prices.json with the product path on every figure. The site answers an automated request with a bot-check page rather than a product, so this was read by hand and is not repeated by any script. A shop price can still move, which is why every figure carries the day it was read.

unownarchives.name: UnownArchives
unownarchives.what: A standing MSRP table for the US, the UK and Europe. Says its US column is read off Pokemon Center US, Target, GameStop and Reddit. Prints no date of its own, which is why the readOn here is the day this repo read it rather than the day it was written.

bujusjujus.name: bujusjujus
bujusjujus.what: An MSRP reference kept by a stock-alert service, which uses the figures to filter out over-priced listings. Says on the page: 'Reviewed July 2026 against Pokemon Center, Best Buy, and GameStop listings.' It is a commercial site with a subscription to sell, which is worth knowing and does not by itself make the table wrong.

billsarchive.name: Bill's Archive
billsarchive.what: A product-by-product MSRP list for the English 30th Celebration line, dated 2 July 2026. Covers one set rather than the whole range, so it corroborates the product types that set sells and says nothing about the rest.

wargamer.name: Wargamer
wargamer.what: A guide to buying at retail price, updated 26 March 2026. Gives approximate figures rather than exact ones ('~$49.99', '~$144'), so it is used to corroborate a figure and never to set one. It is the oldest source here, and the Pokemon Center Elite Trainer Box is one place it has since been overtaken.

products.label: Elite Trainer Box
products.what: The big one. Booster packs, a storage box, sleeves, dice, damage counters and a promo card.
products.note: The most agreed figure on this page, and the one a shop is most likely to be over on. This row said Pokemon Center does not sell the retail box at all, which the fuller reading disproved: it sells five, and every one is old stock. Four Sun and Moon boxes were $39.99 and the Hidden Fates box $49.99 on 17 August 2026. None of them is a current set, so there is still no store reading to check this figure against and it stays on the references.

This row was left blank for a day over that fifty cents, which was the wrong call: twelve listings agreeing is an answer and the outlier belongs in a sentence like this one.
